guides.title: How Is Take-Home Pay Calculated? (2026 Guide)
guides.desc: Learn exactly how your take-home pay is calculated in 2026 — federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare, and state taxes, step by step.
guides.html:
Take-home pay is what lands in your bank account after taxes are withheld from your gross salary. Here is exactly how it is calculated in 2026.

The formula

Take-home pay = gross salary − federal income tax − Social Security − Medicare − state income tax − pre-tax deductions (like 401(k)).

Step 1: Federal income tax

First, subtract the 2026 standard deduction ($16,100 for single filers) from your gross salary to get taxable income. Then apply the progressive federal brackets — only the income inside each bracket is taxed at that bracket’s rate, so your effective rate is lower than your top bracket.

Step 2: FICA (Social Security & Medicare)

Social Security is 6.2% of wages up to the $184,500 wage base. Medicare is 1.45% of all wages, plus an extra 0.9% on income above $200,000 (single). FICA is calculated on gross wages and is not reduced by the standard deduction.

Step 3: State income tax

Most states levy their own income tax on top of federal. Nine states have no wage income tax at all. Rates and brackets vary widely by state.

Step 4: Pre-tax deductions

401(k) and similar contributions reduce your taxable income for income tax (but not for FICA), lowering your tax bill while moving money to retirement.

Want the exact number for your salary and state? Use our free take-home pay calculator.

guides.title: FICA Taxes Explained: Social Security & Medicare (2026)
guides.desc: What is FICA on your paycheck? A clear 2026 explanation of Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) payroll taxes and how much you pay.
guides.html:
FICA stands for the Federal Insurance Contributions Act — the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare. Here is how it works in 2026.

Social Security: 6.2%

Employees pay 6.2% of wages toward Social Security, up to the 2026 wage base of $184,500. Earnings above that are not subject to Social Security tax, so the maximum employee contribution is capped.

Medicare: 1.45% (plus 0.9%)

Medicare is 1.45% of all wages with no cap. High earners pay an additional 0.9% Medicare surtax on income above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (married filing jointly).

Who pays it?

Your employer withholds FICA automatically and matches your Social Security and base Medicare contributions. Self-employed people pay both halves via self-employment tax.

Does 401(k) reduce FICA?

No. Pre-tax 401(k) contributions lower your income tax but not your FICA — Social Security and Medicare apply to your full gross wages.

See your exact FICA withholding with our take-home pay calculator.

guides.title: 2026 Federal Income Tax Brackets (Single Filers)
guides.desc: The 2026 federal income tax brackets and standard deduction, with a clear explanation of how marginal tax rates actually work.
guides.html:
The IRS adjusts tax brackets each year for inflation. Here are the 2026 federal income tax brackets for single filers, plus how they actually apply to your income.

2026 brackets (single filers)

10%$0 – $12,400
12%$12,400 – $50,400
22%$50,400 – $105,700
24%$105,700 – $201,775
32%$201,775 – $256,225
35%$256,225 – $640,600
37%$640,600+

The 2026 standard deduction

$16,100 for single filers, $32,200 for married filing jointly, and $24,150 for heads of household. You subtract this from your income before applying the brackets.

How marginal rates work

Being “in the 22% bracket” does not mean all your income is taxed at 22%. Each portion of income is taxed at its bracket’s rate, so your effective rate is always lower than your top marginal rate.

Source: IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32. Calculate your full tax with our paycheck calculator.

guides.title: States With No Income Tax (2026)
guides.desc: Nine U.S. states have no state income tax in 2026. See which states let you keep more of your paycheck and what to watch out for.
guides.html:
Nine states do not tax wage income in 2026, which means a bigger paycheck than in high-tax states — though they often make up revenue elsewhere.

The nine no-income-tax states

Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, and Wyoming. (New Hampshire repealed its interest-and-dividends tax as of 2025; Washington taxes only certain capital gains, not wages.)

What this means for your paycheck

In a no-income-tax state, your take-home pay is reduced only by federal income tax and FICA. On a $75,000 salary, that can mean roughly $3,000 more per year than in a state like California.

The trade-off

No-income-tax states often have higher sales taxes, property taxes, or other fees. The overall cost of living matters as much as the income tax rate.

guides.title: How to Read Your Paycheck (Pay Stub Explained)
guides.desc: Confused by your pay stub? Here is what each line means — gross pay, federal withholding, FICA, state tax, and net pay.
guides.html:
Your pay stub lists every deduction between your gross salary and the money you actually receive. Here is what each line means.

Gross pay

Your total earnings for the pay period before any deductions — salary or hourly wages times hours worked.

Federal withholding

The federal income tax your employer withholds based on your W-4. It is an estimate of your annual tax, spread across paychecks.

Social Security & Medicare (FICA)

6.2% for Social Security (up to the wage base) and 1.45% for Medicare. These are mandatory payroll taxes.

State & local tax

State income tax where applicable, plus any local or city taxes (for example, New York City or some Ohio municipalities).

Pre-tax deductions

401(k), health insurance premiums, and HSA contributions come out before taxes, lowering your taxable income.

Net pay

What is left — your take-home pay. Check yours against our calculator to make sure your withholding looks right.
